week.t: ISRO fires the rebuilt PSLV third stage (PS3) in a ground static test at Sriharikota, after anomalies on two flights
Science News: ESA’s Hera passed within 30 km of Didymos and Dimorphos on 4 November, the pair whose moon Dimorphos NASA’s DART struck in 2022
NTU and Motherson team up on Spinheat, magnetic nanoparticles that cure coatings from inside: one hour matched 24 in an oven
NASA Earth Observatory: Landsat over Scotland’s Flow Country, peat more than eight metres deep and 9,000 years old
PLOS One: around 60 Natufian clay pieces, 15,000 to 11,600 years old, carry fingerprints, mostly of women and children
Physics World: a white dwarf 282 light-years away is the first genuinely green star known, coloured by calcium and sodium

tiles.cap: A $20,000 humanoid for your home. The catch: a human in a VR headset may be driving it
tiles.nums: joints in each of NEO’s hands, pulled by tendons from motors in the forearm; the whole robot weighs 66 lb (about 30 kg) and runs 4 hours on an 842 Wh battery
tiles.p1: 1X’s NEO is 5 ft 6 in tall, weighs 66 lb and sells for $20,000, or $499 a month, with US deliveries starting in 2026; TIME put it on its Best Inventions 2026 list as the first humanoid robot widely available for the home. The engineering choice that defines it is tendon drive: the motors sit in the forearm and pull tendons through the wrist to 22 joints in each hand, with low gear ratios of about 5:1 to 15:1, so the joints are 95 percent backdrivable, meaning you can push a finger and the motor feels it. A soft lattice-polymer body under a machine-washable knit suit, no pinch points and a walking speed of 1.4 m/s are how 1X says a robot this size can be safe around people.
tiles.p2: The catch reviewers found: for tasks it has not learned, a remote “1X Expert” wearing a VR headset can take over and see through its cameras. Tom’s Guide calls that the one huge problem.
deep: What is inside

An Nvidia Jetson Thor computer, which 1X calls the NEO Cortex, rated at up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS; two 8.85-megapixel stereo fisheye cameras running at 90 Hz; four beamforming microphones; Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and 5G. The 842 Wh battery gives 4 hours of running, and 1X says NEO plugs itself in, gaining an hour of runtime for every 6 minutes of charging.
Numbers from the maker

1X says NEO can lift 154 lb and carry 55 lb, runs at up to 6.2 m/s, moves its hands at up to 8 m/s and makes 22 dB of noise, which it calls quieter than a modern refrigerator. Fingertips push with up to 45 N and position to ±0.2 mm; the hands are rated IP68 against water, the body IP44.
What the critics said

Tom’s Guide’s Jason England: “There is a huge gap between what we are seeing now and what the company is promising.” Only two tasks, answering the door and taking away a cup, are claimed by 1X as autonomous; the rest can be a remote operator, whose view also trains the AI. TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff adds that $499 a month is not a payment plan, you pay until you return it, and “It’s not clear what happens if the robot gets stuck, falls, or accidentally knocks over something.”
A robot that did clean a flat

MIT Technology Review’s Grace Huckins booked a different, remotely piloted humanoid from Tau Robotics this month. On the first visit it failed on carpeted stairs; on the second it cleaned the kitchen but skipped the stove, the toilet brush head fell off three times, taps were left dripping and an oil bottle went over. Her verdict: thorough but slow, and probably a better use of your time to clean yourself.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Amanda Loudin) · 1x.tech NEO spec, order and hands pages · Tom’s Guide (Jason England, 30 Oct 2025) · TechRadar (Lance Ulanoff, 29 Oct 2025) · MIT Technology Review (Grace Huckins, 6 Nov 2026)

tiles.cap: Hera flew within 30 km of the asteroid NASA rammed in 2022. Now the measuring begins
tiles.nums: how close ESA’s Hera came to Didymos and its moon Dimorphos on 4 November, after more than two years in space
tiles.p1: Science News reports that ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the double asteroid Didymos and Dimorphos on 4 November, passing within 30 km after more than two years of travel. It is the first mission to a pair of asteroids orbiting each other; seven single asteroids had been visited before. Dimorphos is the small moon that NASA’s DART spacecraft struck in 2022, shortening its roughly 12-hour orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: Didymos is about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and binary asteroids are thought to make up about 15 percent of all asteroids. If one ever needs nudging, this is the only one anyone has nudged.
deep: Two sides of a coin

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who worked on DART. Hera’s job is to measure what DART left behind and how the pair changed.
A radar lands
In January Hera releases two small companion spacecraft. One, the breadbox-sized Juventas, carries a first-of-its-kind radar to probe the inside of Dimorphos and will attempt a landing on it.
A rubble pile
Dimorphos is thought to be a loose rubble pile like the asteroids Ryugu and Bennu rather than one solid rock; when NASA’s OSIRIS-REx touched Bennu, it sank about half a metre into the surface.
The picture
The image is from Hera’s Asteroid Framing Camera, taken from about 60 km away, and shows the far side of Didymos relative to where DART struck Dimorphos.
tiles.src: Science News, 12 Nov 2026 (Meghan Bartels): Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science
tiles.credit: Photo: ESA (Hera Asteroid Framing Camera), via Science News

tiles.cap: Fingerprints 14,500 years old on a clay torso: an adult’s and a child’s on the same piece
tiles.nums: clay pieces preserving fingerprints, out of about 150 sculpture fragments and tens of thousands of lumps sorted from 40 kg of Natufian clay
tiles.p1: Archaeologists led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem sorted about 40 kilograms of clay from three Natufian sites in present-day Israel, dated between 15,000 and 11,600 years old, where hunter-gatherers were building some of the first permanent settlements. Among tens of thousands of lumps they found about 150 sculpture fragments, including 15 recognisable birds, gazelles and humans, and around 60 pieces that preserve fingerprints. The spacing of the ridges says most of the makers were women and children, some younger than 10, with only a few prints from men.
tiles.p2: One human torso, 14,500 years old, carries the prints of both an adult and a child. Davin suspects an adult teaching a child.
deep: Reading a fingerprint
The spacing between fingerprint ridges is influenced by age and sex, so it gives a rough age and sex. Most of the figurines are under 2 cm long and show little wear.
Hard to find

Concrete evidence of children’s involvement has been hard to find, Davin says. Earlier finds of children’s work Science News lists: rock art about 200,000 years old in Tibet bearing child-sized handprints, and clay sculptures about 30,000 years old in what is now the Czech Republic pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints.
Beyond adult males

It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Michigan. The paper is in PLOS One, 11 November 2026.
The photo
Laurent Davin’s photograph of the sculptures is published under a CC BY 4.0 licence.
tiles.src: Science News, 11 Nov 2026 (Freda Kreier): Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects · PLOS One, Davin et al.
tiles.credit: Photo: Laurent Davin (CC BY 4.0), via Science News

tiles.cap: PSLV’s third stage: anomalies on two flights. ISRO has fired the rebuilt one, bolted down
tiles.nums: maximum thrust of PSLV’s third-stage solid motor, which burns HTPB-based propellant; the whole 44.4 m rocket weighs 320 tonnes at lift-off, says ISRO’s PSLV page
tiles.p1: On Thursday 12 November ISRO carried out a ground static test of the PSLV third stage, PS3, at the Static Test Facility of Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, and called it successful. The test follows anomalies in that stage on two missions, PSLV-C61/EOS-09 and PSLV-C62/EOS-N1; PSLV-C62 lifted off on 12 January this year and, ISRO says, ran into trouble towards the end of the PS3 burn. Since then ISRO has reviewed the stage’s design margins, raw-material acceptance criteria, assembly procedures and quality checks, changed the nozzle configuration to improve design margins, added redundancy in the sealing systems and updated the non-destructive tests done during integration and transport.
tiles.p2: Why now: ISRO said in February that a national-level expert committee was reviewing the anomaly. Its line after Thursday’s test: “Based on the detailed analysis & reviews of the test data, further tests are planned.”
deep: What a solid stage is
PS3 is a solid motor: ISRO’s PSLV page lists it as the S7 motor, burning HTPB-based propellant, with a maximum thrust of 240 kN. A new version of the stage was built for Thursday’s firing.
The January anomaly

ISRO’s PSLV-C62 page says the mission was set to lift off on 12 January 2026 at 10:17 from the First Launch Pad and “encountered an anomaly during end of the PS3 stage”. A detailed analysis was begun, and in February ISRO said a national-level expert committee was reviewing the cause.
Another engine passed

On 5 November, at the ISRO Propulsion Complex in Mahendragiri, the cryogenic engine for the next GSLV flight, GSLV-F19, ran for 200 seconds in its flight acceptance test; both the main engine and the gas generator lit as expected. That engine goes into the stage that will launch the NVS-04 navigation satellite.
The photo
ISRO’s picture shows the static test of the PS3 solid motor under way at Sriharikota on 12 November.
tiles.src: ISRO, 12 Nov 2026: Ground test of third stage of PSLV (PS3) conducted successfully · ISRO PSLV-C62 mission page (8 Jan 2026), PSLV Update (25 Feb 2026) and PSLV configuration page · ISRO, 10 Nov 2026: flight acceptance test of cryogenic engine for GSLV-F19

tiles.cap: Voyager 1 is one light-day away next week. NASA wants your phone to flash it on Tuesday
tiles.nums: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km) from Earth: light, and any radio command, now takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1
tiles.p1: On Wednesday 18 November, NASA says, Voyager 1 will have travelled one light-day from Earth: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km), so far that light from Earth takes 24 hours to reach it. The evening before, Tuesday 17 November, NASA is asking people everywhere to make a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet after sunset, “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day”. A NASA web page makes a phone or tablet flash VGR, Voyager’s call sign, in Morse code.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA announced the activities on Tuesday 10 November. A panel from JPL is streamed on NASA’s site on Friday 20 November at 1 am Singapore time (Thursday noon US Eastern).
deep: Who is talking

The discussion at JPL’s von Kármán Auditorium in Southern California includes Nicky Fox, NASA’s associate administrator for science; Jonathan Lunine, JPL’s chief scientist; Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager; Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager; and Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, the deputy project scientist. It takes questions and is streamed live.
A film is coming
NASA says the event previews a Voyager documentary on NASA+ planned for 2027, the mission’s 50th anniversary.
Which day, exactly

NASA’s invitation says the one-light-day mark falls on Wednesday 18 November, with the light activation the evening before; NASA’s November skywatching page lists the milestone on 17 November. Its chart puts Voyager 1 in the constellation Ophiuchus, toward the western horizon at about 5 pm on the 17th: you cannot see the probe, but you can face it.
Where the picture comes from
The image is an artist’s concept of a Voyager spacecraft from NASA/JPL-Caltech; no camera is out there to photograph it.
tiles.src: NASA release M26-086, 10 Nov 2026 (Gerelle Q. Dodson): NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities · NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026

tiles.cap: Peat covers 3% of land yet holds twice the carbon of every forest. Landsat over Scotland
tiles.nums: of carbon stored in the world’s peatlands, which cover 3 percent of Earth’s land: about twice as much as all the world’s forests combined, says NASA Earth Observatory
tiles.p1: NASA Earth Observatory’s image of 12 November is a Landsat 8 view of the Flow Country in the Scottish Highlands, where peat bogs span about 1,900 square kilometres. Peat is partially decayed plant matter that piles up where soil is so waterlogged that microbes cannot fully break it down; in parts of the Flow Country it has been accumulating for more than 9,000 years and the deposits exceed eight metres in depth. It is the first peatland of its type inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: blanket bogs like this cover roughly 120,000 square kilometres worldwide, under a tenth of one percent of Earth’s land, yet peatlands as a whole hold more than 600 gigatons of carbon.
deep: Blanket

Blanket bogs, also called blanket mires and featherbed bogs, form only where rain is abundant, drainage poor and evaporation low: soggy, treeless land of hummocky mosses, grasses and heathers. The Earth Observatory counts more than 30 species of sphagnum moss in the Flow Country.
Nine thousand years
UNESCO’s figures, quoted by the Earth Observatory: some parts have accumulated peat for more than 9,000 years, and the deposits are more than eight metres thick.
The picture
Landsat 8’s Operational Land Imager acquired the scene on 4 March 2024. The image was made by Michala Garrison with Landsat data from the US Geological Survey; the story is by Adam Voiland.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, 12 Nov 2026 (Adam Voiland; image by Michala Garrison, Landsat 8 OLI, 4 Mar 2024): Scotland’s Flow Country
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, Landsat data from USGS

tiles.cap: Hot things glow red, white, then blue, never green. Then astronomers found a green star
tiles.nums: surface temperature of the white dwarf WDJ1330+6435, about 282 light-years away, which a Warwick team describes as the first genuinely green star known
tiles.p1: Heat anything enough and it glows: a toaster element or a dimmed filament bulb goes dull red, then orange, then white. Physics World’s rule of thumb: about 1,000 K glows red, about 6,000 K white. Stars climb the same ladder from red to orange to white to blue, and no step on that ladder is green: no other star had ever been credibly reported as green. Yet a team led by Mark Hollands at the University of Warwick reports a pale green white dwarf, WDJ1330+6435, about 282 light-years away, with a surface near 4,000 K.
tiles.p2: The trick: calcium and sodium in its atmosphere, debris from asteroids or comets it has swallowed. Sodium normally absorbs a narrow orange, calcium violet; in a white dwarf’s atmosphere, dense at about 1 g/cm³, collisions with the hydrogen and helium atoms broaden the sodium absorption to take in some yellow, lots of orange and some red, and what is left looks pale green.
deep: The test
Find a dimmer switch or watch a toaster element heat up. Note the order of colours, and that there is never a green stage. For a glowing body the colour is set by temperature.
Other odd colours

Physics World notes that carbon-rich white dwarfs look pink or purple, and cooler ones with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres cyan or pale blue. Nearly 400,000 white dwarfs are known, mostly from ESA’s Gaia mission, and about 90 percent have never had their light split into a spectrum.
Who found it

“I have analysed tens of thousands of white dwarf spectra over the years,” says Hollands, whose team publishes in RAS Techniques and Instruments. Of the result: “The resulting mixture of wavelengths results in a pale green colour.”
tiles.src: Physics World, 11 Nov 2026 (Isabelle Dumé): White dwarf star glows an eerie green · RAS Techniques and Instruments

tiles.cap: Why a soap film is striped in colour, and why its thinnest part is black. Test: a cup rim
tiles.nums: of the light hitting a soap film reflects off its front surface; the rest passes in, and some reflects off the back. The two reflections make the colours, says the Exploratorium
tiles.p1: Dip a wire loop or the rim of a cup in bubble solution and hold the film upright against something dark, with a white wall behind you. Bands of colour appear and slide downwards as water drains and the film thins. The Exploratorium’s explanation: light reflecting from the front surface and light reflecting from the back surface recombine; where the extra distance through the film puts the two waves out of step they cancel, and where in step they reinforce. White light with one colour cancelled looks like its opposite: no red gives cyan, no green gives magenta, no blue gives yellow. So a yellow band is where the film’s thickness kills blue.
tiles.p2: The test: watch the top of the film as it thins. It turns black. The film there is so thin that the two reflections cancel for every colour, and you see nothing.
deep: Why black

The front reflection is flipped, because the light is bouncing off a slower medium, air to soap; the back reflection, soap to air, is not. For a film far thinner than a wavelength the two reflections are out of step for every colour, and cancel: black.
The numbers

Soap solution has an index of refraction of about 1.4, so a wavelength inside the film is the air wavelength divided by 1.4. Blue cancels where the film is half a blue wavelength thick, while red is reinforced where the film is a quarter of a red wavelength thick, or a multiple of that. The bands repeat like contour lines as the thickness grows.
The recipe

The Exploratorium’s mix: 2/3 cup (150 mL) of dishwashing liquid and 1 tablespoon of glycerin in 1 gallon (3.8 L) of water, left overnight, which the museum says significantly lengthens the life of the film. A dry finger pops the film; a soap-wetted finger passes through.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Soap Film Painting · Soap Film Interference

tiles.cap: NTU glue cured from inside by magnetic nanoparticles. One hour matched 24 hours in an oven
tiles.nums: adhesive coatings cured by magnetic induction for one hour reached bonding strength comparable to coatings baked in a conventional oven for 24 hours, NTU reports
tiles.p1: Paints, glues and resins on car and aircraft parts are usually cured by putting the whole component into an industrial oven. NTU’s alternative, called Spinheat, mixes specially designed magnetic nanoparticles into the coating; an alternating magnetic field makes the particles generate heat inside the material, so the coating cures from within and heat-sensitive parts are spared. On Thursday NTU announced a partnership with Motherson, a design, engineering and manufacturing company with more than 475 facilities in 47 countries, to take it towards the factory floor.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: in the lab, one hour under the magnetic field matched 24 hours in an oven, and NTU says it could cut energy use, carbon emissions and the space taken up by curing equipment.
deep: Who and how

Professor Raju V. Ramanujan and Associate Professor Terry Steele of NTU’s School of Materials Science and Engineering lead the work; NTU first demonstrated magnetic-field-activated epoxy curing in 2020. The latest version reads the temperature in real time and adjusts the field, delivering heat only when needed, to reduce overheating, bubbles and other defects.
Next

“The next challenge is to understand how this can work reliably within automotive manufacturing,” said Steele. The work is funded by the National Research Foundation under its 29th Competitive Research Programme, was published in Applied Materials Today earlier in 2026, and the intellectual property is filed through NTUitive.
The partner
Motherson makes automotive and aerospace components; Dhruv Mehra, Director of Motherson Singapore, is quoted for the company in the announcement.
tiles.src: NTU News, 12 Nov 2026: NTU, Motherson to develop magnetic technology to cut manufacturing time and energy use

tiles.cap: Paper tube to one eye, other palm beside it, both eyes open: a hole opens in your hand
tiles.nums: the tube’s diameter in the Exploratorium’s recipe: a sheet of A4 or letter paper rolled lengthwise into a tube about 28 cm long, taped shut
tiles.p1: Roll a sheet of paper lengthwise into a tube about 28 cm long and 1.25 cm across and tape it. Hold it in your right hand up to your right eye, both eyes open, and look through it. Now rest your left hand against the left side of the tube about halfway along, fingers pointing up, palm facing you. Your palm appears to have a round hole punched through it. Swap hands and eyes and it happens again.
tiles.p2: Why: one eye sees the hole, the other sees the hand, and your brain fuses the two pictures into a hand with a hole in it.
deep: Make it

The Exploratorium’s recipe is one 8½ × 11 inch sheet of white paper and transparent tape: roll it lengthwise into a tube about 11 inches (28 cm) long and about half an inch (1.25 cm) across, and tape it so it stays rolled.
The dominant eye

Some people find the effect stronger with one eye than the other, the Exploratorium says, because one eye is usually dominant: the brain favours its input. Eye dominance is like handedness, but your dominant eye and dominant hand need not match.
Two pictures, one view
Your two eyes always see slightly different pictures, and your eyes and brain fuse them into one view. Here they are handed a hole and a hand, and fuse those too.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Hole In Your Hand

tiles.cap: The brain’s fear centre is also its save button: how hard it fires decides what you keep
tiles.nums: people with drug-resistant epilepsy, already carrying electrodes to locate their seizures, whose single neurons were recorded while they looked at everyday objects
tiles.p1: Neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and colleagues recorded single neurons in more than 90 people who had electrodes implanted to find the source of their epileptic seizures. Participants viewed images of everyday objects from five categories, such as food and animals, and were asked 10 to 30 minutes later what they remembered. Neurons in the amygdala, two clusters deep in the brain better known for fear, first sorted each image into its category, and the strength of that first response predicted whether the image would be recalled.
tiles.p2: “We forget much of what we experience,” says Xiao; “only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory.” The hippocampus, the usual hero of memory, showed a weaker and slightly delayed link.
deep: Two jobs

The amygdala regulates emotions like fear and aggression; this work, in Nature Neuroscience, adds sorting memories for longer-term storage. Science News also asked cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman of the University of Utah, who was not involved, for his reading.
Why single neurons
The electrodes were there for medicine, to locate seizures before surgery; the memory recordings rode along, a rare chance to listen to individual cells in a living human brain.
Try it on yourself

The finding says the first moment matters: how strongly you sort something when you first see it predicts recall. Next time you meet a new word or formula, say what kind of thing it is before moving on, and check a week later whether it stuck.
tiles.src: Science News, 12 Nov 2026 (Allie Skalnik): The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories · Nature Neuroscience, Xiao et al.

tiles.cap: MIT’s phrase for what a chatbot answer can create: “the illusion of learning”
tiles.nums: principles in MIT’s 2026 report on AI in education
tiles.p1: MIT’s report does not call for banning AI. One of its eight principles is augmentation, not automation: AI should be used to “augment and enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning, not automate them.” Its named risks are the ones you would expect, weaker memory and confidence, falling back on AI at the first hint of struggle, and one you might not: fewer people. MIT saw fewer students at office hours and, anecdotally, fewer in-person groups in dorms and libraries, turning to AI instead of to classmates, TAs or professors.
tiles.p2: The point: the product of school is you, not the mark.
deep: What MIT asks of its own students
Learn to write good prompts, check every output, recognise when it has made something up, and know when not to use it at all.
Why checking matters

The report warns that models hallucinate, so students need to learn when an output is likely to be made up. MIT’s guidance for research: a human is responsible for verifying the output, and AI should never be listed as a co-author.
Keep it human

The report says every subject should include a regular in-person social component, calls for more project-based work, and asks for deliberately AI-free experiences and AI-free spaces for interaction and assessment.
tiles.src: MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training, Aug 2026

tiles.cap: Leonids before dawn Tuesday and Wednesday, up to 15 an hour. Mars meets Jupiter at dawn
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors under ideal skies in the early hours of 17 and 18 November, after the Moon has set; most people will see fewer
tiles.p1: NASA’s skywatching notes for November put the Leonid meteor shower at its best in the early morning hours of Tuesday 17 and Wednesday 18 November, after the Moon sets: up to about 15 meteors an hour under ideal conditions, fewer for most viewers. Around 12 November the Northern Taurids peaked at a gentler 5 an hour. And on the mornings of 15 and 16 November Mars and Jupiter stand about 1.2° apart in the south-east before sunrise, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish beside it.
tiles.p2: Why now: New Moon was 8 November and first quarter is 17 November (US Pacific time); NASA says to look after the Moon sets.
deep: Watch several mornings
NASA suggests watching Mars and Jupiter on more than one morning, to see them close in and then separate again. Jupiter is the brighter of the two.
Three supermoons
The full Moon of 24 November is a supermoon, the first of three in a row: November, December and January. Third quarter follows on 30 November.
Faced the right way
NASA’s chart for 17 November also marks where Voyager 1 sits, in Ophiuchus toward the western horizon at about 5 pm, the day it is a light-day away.
The photo
NASA’s page opens with the full Moon rising over Vasquez Rocks, north of Los Angeles, photographed by Preston Dyches of NASA on 24 June 2021.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A spacesuit, station mould, drinking water: what the crew is packing into Dragon
tiles.nums: in space, across two expeditions, for NASA’s Jessica Watkins on 31 October; the photo shows her marking it with a tray of sweets
tiles.p1: NASA’s station blog for Monday 9 November says the Expedition 75 crew began the week packing a SpaceX Dragon cargo craft to return to Earth next week. Flight engineer Anil Menon examined colonies of bacteria, mould and fungi grown from samples swabbed off station surfaces, measured and photographed them, and packed them for return. Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney unpacked a newly delivered spacesuit, checked it and readied it for the Quest airlock, then moved another suit into Dragon so engineers on the ground can examine it.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: nearly everything that goes up must be counted, swabbed, photographed and, if it is worth the seat, brought back down.
deep: Water and breath

Canadian Space Agency flight engineer Joshua Kutryk collected samples of the station’s drinking water for microbial analysis on Earth. Roscosmos flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov recorded his breathing rate wearing an acoustic monitor around his neck, for research on how weightlessness affects the respiratory system.
Housekeeping in orbit

Station commander Pyotr Dubrov photographed mountains, volcanoes and deserts in South America and Africa. Anna Kikina checked docking mechanisms, cleaned smoke detectors and serviced life-support gear.
What NASA did not say

The blog gives no undocking or splashdown date and no mission number for this Dragon, only “next week”. The crew of seven: Dubrov, Kikina and Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos, Menon, Watkins and Delaney of NASA, and Kutryk of the CSA.
tiles.src: NASA space station blog, 9 Nov 2026: Crew Packing Dragon for Return with Experiments and a Spacesuit

tiles.cap: A $100 kids’ landline: cord, no screen, no apps, Wi-Fi inside. One 7-year-old shrugged
tiles.nums: a month for Tin Can’s Party Line plan, which lets approved ordinary phone numbers call in; Tin Can to Tin Can calls are free
tiles.p1: Tin Can looks like an old desk phone with a curly cord, and that is the point: no screen, no apps, no texting, no games, no internet. Inside it is a Wi-Fi device: it runs on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, plugs into a wall socket, needs no phone line and, as Tom’s Guide’s Mike Prospero explains, makes its calls with VoIP, voice carried over the internet. Only people a parent approves in the companion app can call it or be called; 911 emergency calls are always on. TIME put it on its Best Inventions 2026 list, noting that some 106 countries and 39 US states now restrict phones in schools.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: the engineering is deliberately less. The question is whether a phone that can do only one thing stays interesting.
deep: What is inside

A Wi-Fi radio and a VoIP stack, a speakerphone, voicemail with a greeting you record yourself, speed dial and calling hours set in the app. Prospero compares the idea to MagicJack, the internet-phone gadget of years ago. Tin Can does not publish the handset’s weight or materials. A wired model, Flashback, takes an Ethernet cable instead of Wi-Fi.
The month-long test

Prospero gave one to his 7-year-old. Call quality was “good, but not great”; several voicemails were “crackly, which made them hard to understand”; voicemails can only be heard on the phone, not in the app; and after a month “the novelty of the Tin Can wore off pretty quickly”, and when he suggested calling a friend “she sort of just shrugs.” One parent told him the cords are “waaaaay too easy to unplug.”
The blue-bubble problem

A Tin Can cannot call a child who has a rival kids’ phone such as Pinwheel or Ring Ring: “It’s like a more exclusive version of the blue bubble,” Prospero writes. Tin Can to Tin Can is free; calls with ordinary numbers need the $9.99-a-month Party Line plan, with one free month included.
The maker’s line

“Tech made for kids doesn’t have to be addictive to be useful,” says Tin Can’s About page; the company, Tin Can Untechnologies, is in Seattle. A see-through Technicaller Clear edition with a light-up ringer costs $125.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Emma Barker Bonomo) · tincan.kids product and About pages · Tom’s Guide (Mike Prospero), updated 19 Jul 2026, one-month test

tiles.cap: NTU’s AI steers planes round moving thunderstorms. In the busiest tests, none got close
tiles.nums: of eight aircraft reached their goal in the same storms where four aircraft scored 100%; in the most crowded tests separation between planes was never lost
tiles.p1: Thunderstorms force controllers to reroute planes, and climate change is bringing more severe weather, writes NTU’s engineering school. The team of Associate Professor Sameer Alam, director of NTU’s Air Traffic Management Research Institute, built a cooperative AI, with the unlovely name IDDPG, a multi-agent framework that keeps aircraft a safe distance from thunderstorm cells and from each other while minimising total flight distance. In a 200 by 200 nautical mile box with two storm cells drifting northwest to southeast over 30 minutes, four aircraft from three entry points all got through safely; with eight aircraft the goal-reach rate fell to 95 percent and flight distances grew slightly.
tiles.p2: Why here: the test airspace was a real en route area of the Singapore flight information region, the sky our controllers manage.
deep: Pushing it

“We wanted to push the model to its limits,” Alam says. In six scenarios from one small cell to three large moving cells, performance declined as complexity rose and improved when storm tracks were known in advance. In the most crowded scenarios the goal-reach rate stayed at 98 to 99 percent and separation was never lost.
The weak spot
Uncertainty about when each plane arrives. The team tested four levels of estimated-time-of-arrival uncertainty, from negligible to high, and high uncertainty significantly degraded performance.
Why not one brain

Existing automation tools, the team says, are not scalable or efficient enough for fast-changing weather, and a single-agent approach limits cooperative decisions. “Our aim is to find an optimal solution to ensure safe separation distance among multiple aircraft,” Alam says.
Where it is published

Advanced Engineering Informatics 2025 (Pang, Hu, Zhang, Alam, Lulli) and the AAMAS 2026 conference on autonomous agents in Paphos, Cyprus. The article appeared on NTU’s mechanical and aerospace engineering news page on 4 November.
